title.en: Explain the concern for future generations
State Herman Daly's conditions for sustainable development

say.en: If we use up all the groundwater and forests today, our grandchildren inherit a desert. Can we grow without borrowing from them? In this lesson: Define sustainable development.
Explain the concern for future generations.
State Herman Daly's conditions for sustainable development.

body.en: The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development defined *sustainable development* as development that meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The Brundtland Commission emphasised protecting future generations: we have a moral obligation to hand over the earth in good order, leaving them at least the same stock of quality-of-life assets that we inherited. Sustainable development also aims at decreasing absolute poverty by providing lasting and secure livelihoods that minimise resource depletion, environmental degradation, cultural disruption and social instability.

points.en: Meet present needs without compromising future generations
Leave future generations at least what we inherited
Reduce poverty through lasting, secure livelihoods

narration.en: Sustainable development meets our needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. We must leave them at least as much as we received, and reduce poverty through lasting livelihoods.

narration.en: Let us build the idea of sustainable development and Daly's five conditions.

say.en: Draw two generations: the present and the future. Development must serve both.
Meet today's needs, but hand over at least as much to the next generation.
Herman Daly gave five conditions. One: keep the population within the carrying capacity.
Two: technology should be input-efficient. Three: harvest renewables no faster than they regenerate.
Four: use up non-renewables no faster than we create renewable substitutes. Five: correct the damage from pollution.
Let us build the idea of sustainable development and Daly's five conditions.

caption.en: A lake's fish stock regrows each year, fastest at half its full size. If the yearly catch stays within what the stock can regrow, fishing can go on for ever. Catch more than the regrowth and the stock collapses, leaving nothing for future generations.

body.en: *Herman* Daly, a leading environmental economist, said that to achieve sustainable development we must: limit the human population to a level within the carrying capacity of the environment; make technological progress input-efficient and not input-consuming; extract renewable resources on a sustainable basis, that is, at a rate not exceeding the rate of regeneration; keep the rate of depletion of non-renewable resources no higher than the rate of creation of renewable substitutes; and correct the inefficiencies arising from pollution.

narration.en: Daly gave five conditions: keep population within carrying capacity, use input-efficient technology, harvest renewables no faster than they regrow, replace non-renewables with renewable substitutes at least as fast as we use them up, and correct pollution.
narration.kn: ಡೇಲಿ ಐದು ಷರತ್ತುಗಳನ್ನು ನೀಡಿದರು: ಜನಸಂಖ್ಯೆ ಧಾರಣ ಸಾಮರ್ಥ್ಯದೊಳಗಿರಲಿ, ಸಮರ್ಥ ತಂತ್ರಜ್ಞಾನ, ಪುನರುತ್ಪಾದನೆ ಮೀರದ ಬಳಕೆ, ಬದಲಿ ಸಂಪನ್ಮೂಲ ಸೃಷ್ಟಿ, ಮಾಲಿನ್ಯ ನಿವಾರಣೆ.

problem.en: A village forest regrows 500 tonnes of wood a year, but the villagers cut 650 tonnes a year. Is this sustainable? What is the largest sustainable cut?

steps.en: Daly's condition for renewables: extraction must not exceed regeneration.
Here extraction 650 > regeneration 500, so the stock falls by 650 − 500 = 150 tonnes every year.
The forest will keep shrinking, so this is not sustainable.
The largest sustainable cut is 500 tonnes a year, equal to regrowth.

answer.en: Not sustainable: the stock falls by 150 tonnes a year. A cut of at most 500 tonnes a year is sustainable.

Daly's condition for renewables: extraction must not exceed regeneration.
Here extraction 650 is greater than regeneration 500, so the stock falls by 650 minus 500 equals 150 tonnes every year.
The forest will keep shrinking, so this is not sustainable.
The largest sustainable cut is 500 tonnes a year, equal to regrowth.
So the answer is Not sustainable: the stock falls by 150 tonnes a year. A cut of at most 500 tonnes a year is sustainable.
